sources.title: Kang Youwei (Q360135), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Kang Youwei', description 'Chinese politician and scholar (1858-1927)', instance of human, born 19 March 1858, died 31 March 1927 (a second death-date claim says 28 February), citizen of the Qing dynasty and the Republic of China, occupations including politician, philosopher and scholar, Korean label 캉유웨이. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kang Youwei' (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him a Chinese scholar, a leader of the Reform Movement of 1898 and a key figure in the intellectual development of modern China; records his 1883 attempt to end foot-binding in his village, the school he opened in Guangzhou, his books on the forged classics and on Confucius as a reformer, his mobilising of provincial graduates against the 1895 peace terms, the Society for the Study of National Strengthening (suppressed 1896), the 1898 reform programme, his flight, the Reform Association founded abroad, the reformers' failed 1900 revolts, his writing of the utopian Datongshu, his return in 1913 and part in the abortive 1917 restoration of the Qing ruler; notes that critics charge he invoked Confucius to serve his aims and that partisan writers attacked his later positions. Reference entry, unsigned on the page.

'K'ang Yu-wei', Encyclopedia of World Biography (Gale, unsigned), on Encyclopedia.com (read in full). A longer reference biography with a frank assessment: his 1878 emotional crisis and withdrawal, the 1891 Canton school with Liang Qichao among its students, the 1895 petition against the Treaty of Shimonoseki (it says nearly 1,300 signed; later scholars give different counts), the Society for the Study of National Strengthening founded in 1895 and banned in 1896, his short books on Peter the Great and the Meiji Restoration for the Guangxu Emperor, the 1898 audience and decrees, his escape on a British gunboat, the Baohuanghui of 1899, travels to India, Europe and the United States, harsh attacks on anti-Manchu revolutionaries, his support for the 1917 restoration and his appeals to warlords in 1923; calls him a man of 'monumental egotism and arrogance' who seldom acknowledged intellectual debts, and says by 1927 most Chinese intellectuals saw him as a relic.

Hao Chang, 'Kang Yuwei', Encyclopedia of Religion (Gale, 2005 edition), on Encyclopedia.com (read in full). Scholarly reference entry by a historian of modern Chinese thought: describes his spiritual crisis before twenty, his reinterpretation of Confucianism around human-heartedness and the three-age scheme, his campaign to make Confucianism a state religion, his leading of the 1898 reform and Cixi's reversal, his exile with Liang Qichao until 1913, his resumed Confucian campaign and his joining Zhang Xun's failed 1917 restoration; judges the reinterpretation bold but its influence short-lived. Overlaps with the other reference entries.

Mao Haijian, 'Wuxu shiqi Kang Youwei yu Guangxu di' (Kang Youwei and the Guangxu Emperor in the 1898 period), Jindaishi yanjiu (Modern Chinese History Studies) 2021, no. 4, read in Chinese through the author-authorised repost on Aisixiang. A leading scholar's archive-based article that starts from the finding that Kang's Wuxu zougao memorials were forged about 1911, that his autobiography Wo shi is unreliable and that Liang Qichao's account exaggerates, and then rebuilds what the surviving documents show: the 1888 memorial that the Imperial College and the Censorate would not forward, five memorials Kang ghost-wrote for censors, the May 1895 assembly of provincial graduates (602 signatories) and the memorial that reached the Emperor on 3 June, his one audience on 16 June 1898, 18 memorials passed up through the Zongli Yamen and a grand councillor and collected by the Emperor as 'Outstanding Scholar's memorials', the Emperor's later edicts drawn on them (the author counts 8 of 27 reform items from Kang's group), the Emperor's shielding of Kang, and the 1898 edict that charged him. Concludes Kang remained one of the main drivers of the reform.

Mao Haijian, 'Wuxu bianfa qijian de baoju' (Recommendations during the Hundred Days' Reform), Lishi yanjiu (Historical Research) 2006, no. 6, read in Chinese through the author-authorised repost on Aisixiang. Archive-based article on how Kang's circle got to the Emperor: the 1897 recommendation that he join a peace-arbitration society, the April 1898 recommendation by Xu Zhijing, other recommenders, the July 1898 wave of recommending memorials that, with Kong Xiangji, the author judges Kang's group drafted themselves, Kang's dissatisfaction with the secretary post he was given, the order to leave for Shanghai that, a hostile memorial complained, he did not obey at once, and his last attempts to find foreign help. Concludes that Kang exaggerated and was politically naive, that his self-promotion through intermediaries could be faulted but was a legitimate strategy for a junior man, and that without Kang's circle there would have been no reform.

Luke S. K. Kwong's letter and Young-tsu Wong's reply, 'Communications to the Editor', Journal of Asian Studies (pp. 402-412; a scholarly exchange over Wong's 1992 article 'Revisionism Reconsidered: Kang Youwei and the Reform Movement of 1898'; read in full). Kwong argues that Kang's and Liang Qichao's accounts contain half-truths and that Kang's role was smaller than the traditional account (for example, the audience Kang described as lasting two and a half hours lasted about ten minutes according to Zhang Yuanji, who was received the same day, and Kang's 1888 memorial was refused partly for its scathing tone toward Cixi and the Emperor); Wong replies that Kang was already a scholar-celebrity by 1895 and a central, though not mastermind, figure. Used as the adversarial scholarly counter-voice.

The World's Work, vol. XII (May-October 1906; Doubleday, Page and Co., New York; scan from the Robarts Library, University of Toronto, on the Internet Archive; plate and article read). Contains the captioned portrait plate 'Kang Yu Wei, the eminent Chinese reformer ... ordered to be executed in 1898, but escaped', credited 'Photograph copyrighted 1905 by E. Chickering Co.', and Kang's own article 'The Hostility of China' (pp. 7487 ff., written in Mexico) on the American boycott, in which he reports an American's argument about Filipino exclusion that was 'novel' to him and which he finds has 'much force'. The article is Kang's own account and is used for his stated reasoning only.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_kang_britannica, src_kang_mao2021, src_kang_mao2006, src_kang_gale | 1883-1899 | reference biography, scholarly paper, scholarly paper, reference biography] He tried to end foot-binding in his village in 1883, opened a school, wrote seven memorials to the throne although as a junior man he had no right to submit them, ghost-wrote memorials for censors, organised provincial graduates in 1895, founded study and reform societies, sent books to the Emperor, and after the 1898 coup founded an exile association. The initiatives are documented in reference biographies and, with the self-serving details stripped out, in two archive-based scholarly papers.

persistence.rationale: [src_kang_mao2021, src_kang_britannica, src_kang_gale | 1888-1923 | scholarly paper, reference biography, reference biography] After the 1888 memorial was refused he found other routes (ghost-written memorials, more petitions, books, societies), after the 1896 ban on his society he founded another, after the 1898 coup he spent years building an exile association, and he joined the 1917 restoration and approached warlords in 1923. The pattern across failures is documented by several works; the later stretch rests on the reference entries, and holding to the monarchist line after 1912 is part of why his influence shrank. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent, source concentration): The 1888-1898 stretch is documented by scholarly papers, but the exile years and the 1917 and 1923 episodes rest on the reference entries alone.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_kang_mao2021, src_kang_gale, src_kang_kwong | 1895-1898 | scholarly paper, reference biography, scholarly paper] The Society for the Study of National Strengthening drew in prominent officials, the Emperor had his memorials copied, adopted several of his proposals as edicts and shielded him from attacks, and Li Hongzhang wrote that the edicts came largely from Kang's and Liang's urging. Against that, the Zongli Yamen refused his institutional plan, the 1888 memorial was refused for its tone, and Kwong doubts accounts of his oratory and his audience. Moderate, because the evidence is contested. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): Much of the case for his influence is contested between Kwong and Wong, and the 'tears at his speeches' accounts come from his own and Liang's problematic sources.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_kang_mao2021, src_kang_mao2006, src_kang_britannica | 1895-1898 | scholarly paper, scholarly paper, reference biography] He founded or led reform societies, proposed that a new 'institutions bureau' sit in the palace and meet the Emperor daily so that he could direct the reform, was dissatisfied with the junior secretary post he was given, and his circle pressed recommendations to bring him and his followers into a policy-making body. The wish to hold the lead is documented in the two archive-based papers; how far he actually led events is disputed (Kwong). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): Mao documents the wish to head a policy body, but Kwong and Mao both stress how little control he had over events.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_kang_mao2006, src_kang_mao2021, src_kang_britannica | 1888-1900 | scholarly paper, scholarly paper, reference biography] He submitted a memorial in 1888 that criticised the two highest figures of the court bluntly, pressed his programme in 1898 when senior officials were hostile, stayed in Beijing, as a hostile memorial complained, after he was ordered to go to Shanghai, and (per Britannica) belonged to a reform camp that instigated failed revolts in 1900. The first three points are documented by scholars; the last rests on one reference entry. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): The 1900 revolts are given by one reference entry, and the 1888 memorial's risk is Kwong's reading of its tone.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_kang_mao2021, src_kang_gale, src_kang_britannica | 1894-1912 | scholarly paper, reference biography, reference biography] In 1894 a censor demanded that his book be destroyed and the throne ordered an inquiry, yet he went on publishing; in 1898 senior officials and censors attacked him repeatedly; in exile he wrote harsh attacks on anti-Manchu revolutionaries and competed sharply with them for overseas support. Documented by three works that overlap, so a strong inference. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent, source concentration): The three works overlap (one reference family plus one scholarly paper), and the competition with revolutionaries is given only in general terms.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_kang_gale, src_kang_britannica, src_kang_chang, src_kang_mao2021 | 1878-1897 | reference biography, reference biography, reference biography, scholarly paper] He broke with the examination-bound scholarship of his upbringing, argued that the orthodox classics had been tampered with and that Confucius was a reformer, and was denounced in 1894 for it. The rejection of orthodoxy is documented in print and in the 1894 denunciation; the characterisation of his motives comes mainly from reference entries that draw on one body of scholarship. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent, source concentration): The three reference entries and the scholarly paper draw on one body of scholarship, and the account of his motives is a reference-entry characterisation.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_kang_britannica, src_kang_gale, src_kang_chang | 1883-1913 | reference biography, reference biography, reference biography] His first reform attempt was local (foot-binding in 1883), then national memorials, a school teaching new learning, societies, newspapers and overseas schools and a business firm, all aimed at changing outcomes; his utopian Datongshu he withheld because he thought the public unready. The pattern is documented, but the three entries draw on the same scholarship, so confidence is moderate. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent, source concentration): The three reference entries overlap; only the 1883 foot-binding attempt is given by a single entry, so the pattern is moderately supported.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_kang_mao2021, src_kang_mao2006, src_kang_kwong | 1888-1898 | scholarly paper, scholarly paper, scholarly paper] With no right to memorialise, he ghost-wrote memorials for censors, used officials and the Zongli Yamen to pass up his own, courted patrons (Kwong adds his ties to Zhang Yinhuan), and, per Mao and Kong Xiangji, his circle drafted the recommending memorials that promoted them. Several scholars document workarounds; ghost-writing for one's own promotion cuts both ways.

achievement_drive.rationale: [src_kang_mao2006, src_kang_kwong, src_kang_gale | 1888-1898 | scholarly paper, scholarly paper, reference biography] Mao records that Kang was dissatisfied with the junior secretary post and wanted a central role; his circle drafted memorials recommending themselves; Kwong shows that he gave an inflated figure for the length of his only audience; the Gale entry calls him a man of 'monumental egotism and arrogance'. Ambition and self-presentation are documented in two scholarly papers; the Gale judgement is an unsupported characterisation. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent, source concentration): One scholar's report of his dissatisfaction with a post, one scholar's correction of his audience figure, and a reference entry's unsupported character judgement; no direct statement of his aims.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: STRONG (Stage B) / lead SURVIVED: the Chickering photograph printed in The World's Work vol. XII (1906). I viewed the plate itself at 2527 x 3700 px: the printed caption reads 'KANG YU WEI', says he was ordered executed in 1898 but escaped, and the credit line reads 'Photograph copyrighted 1905 by E. Chickering Co.'; the page-number index shows the plate precedes p. 7472 and the caption points to his own article at p. 7487. Commons file 'Portrait of Kang Youwei.jpg' (1047 x 1563) cites the same plate; I used the Internet Archive scan directly and did not rely on the Commons template. LOC item 2005688106 (read through its JSON endpoint) is a different pose of the same 1905 Chickering session ('Yu Wei Kang, 1858-1927 ... Copyright by Chickering', c1905, caption-card data marked unverified) and is a cross-check on photographer and year only. Chickering d. 1915 (Wikidata description). KIND likeness: a studio photograph from his 1905 United States stay. TERMS: IA terms page is script-rendered and unreadable; item metadata has no rights statement; rights rest on pre-1931 US publication and creator death. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-24, Wikidata API) Q360135 'Kang Youwei', 'Chinese politician and scholar (1858-1927)', human, b. 1858-03-19, d. 1927-03-31 (a second death claim of 02-28; Britannica says 21 March). REGION east_asia. ERA 20th_century (died 1927; precedent Zhan Tianyou, Wang Guowei). Nationality CN. ATTRIBUTION: attributable, but his own accounts (Wo shi, forged Wuxu zougao, Liang's Wuxu zhengbian ji) are unreliable per Mao and Kwong, so no row relies on them. BELIEFS UNSCORED: his Confucian-religion programme, constitutional-monarchist politics, opposition to the republic and utopian Datong ideas are not scored; only documented conduct (memorials and ghost-writing, organising, flight, exile association, the 1917 and 1923 episodes as perseverance). Nothing endorses or condemns his politics. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Britannica entry. READ (8 sources besides Wikidata): Britannica (full, fetched with an honest user agent, no bot wall), Gale Encyclopedia of World Biography entry (full), Hao Chang's Encyclopedia of Religion entry (full), Mao Haijian 2021 (large part, Chinese), Mao Haijian 2006 (conclusion and middle sections, Chinese), Kwong-Wong exchange in the Journal of Asian Studies (full), The World's Work plate and Kang's own 1906 article. Not used: OAPEN open-access book on the Baohuanghui (Anubis bot wall), Project MUSE, CORE and Hawaii ScholarSpace PDFs (bot walls), Stanford UP excerpt (429), and the BC Studies paper on Sun Yat-sen read only for context. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: petition signatories are given as 602 (Mao), nearly 1,300 (Gale) or hundreds (Britannica), so none is printed as fact except attributed; the school opening year is 1890 (Britannica) or 1891 (Gale) and is left vague; Kang's audience length is 2.5 hours by his account and about ten minutes per Zhang Yuanji; how large his role in 1898 was is disputed between Kwong (smaller) and Wong and Mao (a main driver). Adversarial voices: Kwong, and Mao's finding that Kang forged later memorials and exaggerated. Not checked: Kang's autobiography, Liang's biography, Hsiao Kung-chuan, the Larson and Worden book on the Baohuanghui (bot wall), and the alleged fund-raising abuses of the Baohuanghui (only a non-scholarly source found, not used). SELF-CALIBRATION: eight rows lowered, five of them for source concentration. KO NAME: 캉유웨이 (Korean Wikipedia title and Wikidata ko label; the Sino-Korean 강유위 is also found in Korean encyclopedic texts; repo precedent for this period is the Chinese reading, as in 쑨원, 왕궈웨이).

portrait.source: Full-page plate 'Kang Yu Wei' (caption: the eminent Chinese reformer, a believer in Western methods and Western institutions, who was ordered to be executed in 1898, but escaped; credit line 'Photograph copyrighted 1905 by E. Chickering Co.') in The World's Work, vol. XII, May-October 1906 (New York: Doubleday, Page and Co.), unnumbered plate facing p. 7472 and referred to p. 7487 where Kang's own article appears; scan from the Robarts Library, University of Toronto, on the Internet Archive (item worldswork12gard, leaf 16). I viewed the plate image itself, not only the OCR. The photograph was cropped from the plate scan (2106 x 3146 px) and downscaled to 669 x 1000 px; not upscaled.
portrait.license: Public domain in the United States by age of publication: the photograph by Elmer Chickering (1857-1915), copyrighted 1905 by E. Chickering Co., was published in New York in 1906, before 1931, and its photographer died more than 70 years ago. The rights basis is the publication date and creator death, not a Commons template. The Internet Archive item record carries no rights statement; its terms page is script-rendered and could not be read (no rights conflict found).
